articles.title_orig: King, dingers power Padres in G1 rout at frenzied Petco
articles.title_zh: King, dingers power Padres in G1 rout at frenzied Petco
articles.content_orig:
SAN DIEGO -- They packed Petco Park anticipating a party in the Gaslamp on Tuesday night. The Cubs could do little to stop it. The Padres wouldn't let it end.
Three pitches into the top of the first inning, Michael King punched out Pete Crow-Armstrong. The ballpark erupted. Eight pitches later, King had retired the side in order. Louder, still. Leading off the bottom of the first, Fernando Tatis Jr. crushed the first pitch he saw over the center-field wall. Somehow, even louder.
That noise reached a crescendo two batters later, when Manny Machado launched another home run off Cubs left-hander Matthew Boyd . The Padres were well on their way to an 8-0 victory in Game 1 of the National League Wild Card Series. The party in downtown San Diego never stopped.
“The crowd was great,” said Cubs manager Craig Counsell. “... They had a lot to cheer about tonight -- and we didn't give them anything to be quiet about.”
King would carry a no-hitter into the seventh. By the time Nico Hoerner broke up King’s bid at history with a soft single down the third-base line with one out in the seventh, the Padres had built a 7-0 lead. It was the longest individual postseason no-hit bid since Aníbal Sánchez went 7 2/3 for the Nationals in the 2019 NLCS. King would finish with seven innings of one-hit ball.
Postseason Guide • Final bracket • Wild Card Series matchups • How to watch Wild Card Series on NBC, Peacock • Postseason schedule
King would allow just that one hit over seven innings -- 28 years to the day that Kevin Brown punched out 16 Astros in the 1998 NLDS. That game is widely regarded as the greatest single-game pitching performance in franchise history. King made a strong case for No. 2.
The game stood in stark contrast to last year’s Wild Card Series between these two teams, which Chicago controlled throughout. Suddenly, the Cubs’ backs are against the wall. And the Padres are one win from a trip to Milwaukee and the NLDS.
“Obviously we've got to continue doing it,” Machado said. “Not all games are going to be like the one today. But we're always ready for the battle.”
Here are some takeaways from Game 1:
1. This is a very different Padres offense
Maybe a few of the names are the same. But this is not the Padres offense that scored all of five runs across three games in last year’s Wild Card Series at Wrigley Field.
For a month now, the Padres have been the best offense in baseball. And if there were any doubt whether that would carry over into October … the Padres erased it with a couple swings in the bottom of the first inning.
"We’re one. We’re coming together as one group," Tatis said. "At-bat after at-bat, we trust each other."
Tatis and Machado became the first Padres teammates to combine for multiple home runs in the first inning of a playoff game in franchise history. Xander Bogaerts would add a homer of his own in the fourth. The Padres poured it on.
By the fifth inning Tuesday night they’d scored more than they had in that entire three-game series at Wrigley Field a year ago.
“We did a good job with Tatis last year,” Counsell said. “We did not do a good job today, and it starts with that.”
Indeed, Tatis struggled last postseason -- and seemed to be at the center of everything on Tuesday night. But beyond that, the Padres offense is just … deeper this year. There are more levers to pull, and Stammen has been pulling them.
2. Boyd’s changeup betrays him
One of the keys to Boyd being as effective and consistent as he has been for the Cubs is the reliability of his changeup. It is his signature offspeed offering, but the lefty’s command of the pitch eluded him in Game 1 and it proved costly.
All three home runs surrendered by Boyd came off his changeup, marking the first time in his career (regular season or postseason) that he allowed that many homers in a game off that pitch. The blasts from Tatis, Machado and Bogaerts each came off changeups that were left in the strike zone.
“When it comes down to it, I just wasn’t as sharp with my changeup,” Boyd said. “It could have been better. They definitely could’ve been better. A team like that, especially Machado and Tatis, they’re going to be aggressive. I just didn’t throw it where I wanted to and they hit the mistakes.”
While allowing homers was an issue for the Cubs’ staff this season – their 231 homers surrendered led the NL – Boyd was one of the better performers on that front. In fact, the lefty allowed no homers in September, only two in his final seven starts combined and only allowed two or more in a game in three of his 22 starts.
3. Michael King might’ve done more than just win Game 1
The Padres have the sport's best bullpen. But how much stress could it handle across three games this week?
Well, now they really only need to worry about two -- at most.
Not only was King electric. The fact that he covered seven innings -- not to mention the tack-on runs from the Padres offense -- could go a long way toward helping them win the series. Mason Miller and Adrian Morejon are still fresh. The whole bullpen is, really.
The Cubs’ uphill climb in Games 2 and 3 just got a whole lot steeper. A red-hot Nick Pivetta gets the ball in Game 2 -- and Stammen can turn to his high-leverage arms whenever he needs to.
4. Cubs needed their lineup to step up
The Cubs ended the season leading the Major Leagues in runs scored (850), walks (674), slugging percentage (.428) and OPS (.767), while pacing the NL in home runs (220). A deep October run was going to be contingent on that offense continuing to roll, given the rocky nature of Chicago’s pitching.
Game 1 against the Padres could not have gone worse in that regard for the North Siders. The Cubs went 0-for-20 into the seventh inning before Hoerner’s infield single. Chicago’s dynamic one-two punch of Crow-Armstrong and Alex Bregman finished a combined 0-for-7 with six strikeouts.
“He was really good. Tip your cap,” Bregman said of King. “He threw the ball really well. Had everything really working and we didn’t do, really, anything right today. The good news is we get to show up tomorrow and play a baseball game. We’ve just got to execute better in all phases of the game.”

articles.title_orig: iOS 26.7.1—Update Now Warning Issued To iPhone Users
articles.title_zh: iOS 26.7.1—Update Now Warning Issued To iPhone Users
articles.content_orig:
Attackers are exploiting CVE-2026-86950, an out-of-bounds write flaw, in an extremely sophisticated fashion, according to Apple.
Apple released new versions of iOS and macOS to address a zero-day vulnerability that a threat actor is actively exploiting in targeted attacks.
The out-of-bounds write vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-86950 , affects Apple's CoreGraphics framework, which macOS and iOS use to render and manipulate 2D graphics. The vulnerability affects a broad range of Apple devices, including iPhones dating back to the iPhone 11 and multiple generations of iPads.
The flaw has a CVSS score of 8.8 and can allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code on an affected system. According to Apple's advisory , the vulnerability is being exploited "in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals" on versions of iOS before iOS 27. The technology giant said it has addressed the vulnerability by adding checks to ensure the software does not write data beyond the memory allocated for it.
Related: South Africa Seeks Help After Cyberattack Targets Air Traffic Control
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-86950 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog — a source that it wants organizations to use to prioritize patching efforts . In keeping with its binding operative directive (BOD 26-04) from earlier this year for high-priority vulnerabilities, CISA has given federal civilian executive branch agencies three days to apply Apple's recommended mitigation for the vulnerability. As per BOD 26-04, these agencies must also conduct a forensic triage by Oct. 2 to determine if they have already been compromised via CVE-2026-86950.
Apple credited Meta with disclosing the vulnerability to the company but has not released any information on the exploit activity or who it might be targeting.
Adam Bynton, enterprise security manager at Jamf, says CVE-2026-86950 is significant because it affects a component of the graphics stack used to process content across Apple's operating systems. Though Apple has only referenced the attacks as targeting iOS, the company has patched the same flaw in macOS Tahoe and Sequoia, Boynton points out.
“The broader pattern is worth watching," he says. "We continue to see highly sophisticated attacks look for routes through components that process untrusted content." As an example, he pointed to CVE-2025-55177 , a vulnerability in WhatsApp that attackers exploited in combination with CVE-2025-43300 , another out-of-bounds zero-day vulnerability, this time in Apple's ImageIQ technology.
"We have also seen Apple disclose targeted exploitation involving WebKit and other memory-safety vulnerabilities," Boynton says.
Related: AI Sandbox Escapes: Why Forensic Readiness Matters More Than Containment
That shouldn’t be interpreted as Apple devices being broadly insecure, he says. "Apple describes these attacks as highly sophisticated and targeted at a very small population, which is why separating targeted exploitation from everyday enterprise risk is important.”
It's unclear who is exploiting CVE-2026-86950 and if the attacks are ongoing. But Apple's description of the attacks as being extremely sophisticated hints that a nation-state actor or spyware firm might be involved. WhatsApp, for instance, has previously accused Israel's NSO Group of using its servers to distribute its Pegasus spyware on mobile devices belonging to targeted individuals.
Ensar Seker, chief information security officer at SOCRadar, says a memory-corruption vulnerability like CVE-2026-86950, which can lead to arbitrary code execution during file processing, creates the potential for a low-interaction or potentially zero-click attack chain when combined with an appropriate delivery mechanism.
The other important detail is Apple's description of the exploitation as an "extremely sophisticated attack" against specific individuals, he says. "That language generally points toward highly targeted operations rather than broad cybercrime," he adds. "Organizations should therefore treat this less like a theoretical vulnerability and more like an indication that advanced threat actors continue to invest heavily in finding ways around Apple's security architecture."
Related: SectopRAT Returns, Hiding Inside a Legitimate Application
The trend is not simply that Apple has more vulnerabilities, Seker continues. What stands out is the continued discovery of flaws being used in sophisticated exploit chains targeting devices that many organizations have traditionally viewed as lower-risk endpoints.
"Over the past year, we have seen exploited vulnerabilities involving WebKit, media and image processing, privilege escalation, authorization controls, and memory corruption," Seker says. "Attackers are increasingly looking for chains rather than a single vulnerability: One flaw provides initial code execution, another escapes a sandbox or increases privileges, and additional components establish access to sensitive information."
The fact that Apple devices are strategically important endpoints at many enterprises, and many high-value targets frequently use iPhones and Macs, also makes the economics of developing exploits targeting Apple vulnerabilities more attractive. The first priority for organizations therefore is to reduce patch latency for Apple products. "When Apple identifies active exploitation, security teams should treat the update as an emergency security patch rather than waiting for the normal monthly patching cycle," Seker says.Organizations should also bring Apple devices fully into their enterprise security program and stop treating them as inherently secure endpoints simply because of Apple's security architecture. "Enterprises need centralized device management, enforced OS minimum versions, rapid update policies, visibility into device compliance, and controls that prevent outdated devices from accessing sensitive corporate resources," he says.
Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.
Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.
Jai previously served as senior editor at Computerworld, where he covered information security and data-privacy issues. His work has also appeared in CSO Online, InformationWeek, The Christian Science Monitor Passcode, The Economic Times, and other publications.
His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Anthropic IPO prospectus lays bare deep dependence on Big Tech partners
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Anthropic IPO prospectus lays bare deep dependence on Big Tech partners
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic says its AI models could pose a “catastrophic or existential risk to humanity” and can “resist shutdown,” according to an initial public offering prospectus obtained by Reuters.
Anthropic is pursuing an IPO some time in the next year that many expect to value the five-year-old company at approximately $2 trillion. The company’s Wall Street debut will follow a June public offering by SpaceX, which owed much of its $2 trillion opening day valuation to its own AI efforts. OpenAI , the other leading American AI company, has announced plans for its own public offering.
The Anthropic IPO could raise tens of billions of dollars for the cash-hungry company. But the company behind Claude also warned in the prospectus that its AI models can have “self-preserving behaviors” and have attempted to “conceal or manipulate information” and engaged in behavior “resembling blackmail” according to the report.
Why AI companies are choosing to go public
The run of AI public offerings not only gives individual and institutional investors a chance to cash in on the AI boom, but also provides more transparency about their businesses. Yet the IPOs come amid growing concerns about AI’s advancement and capabilities.
An AI agent from OpenAI, Anthropic’s chief rival, broke into an Australian healthcare database, the country’s prime minister revealed last week. OpenAI also disclosed Friday that its agents probed three US government websites without authorization, but in that case did not obtain non-public data.
In a prospectus, companies typically offer investors lists of risks they face, such as lawsuits and competitive pressures, when laying out the case for investing in the company. But the hazards are never this stark. Anthropic dedicated 80 pages to its risk factors in the leaked prospectus, significantly more than the 48 pages it spent detailing its business, according to Reuters.
Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment from CNN.
The prospectus is likely to feed growing concerns about the risks posed to humanity by AI. Earlier this month, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon received widespread attention when he left the company and posted on X that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
Anthropic is one of the leading companies in AI development, and its CEO Dario Amodei responded to Coxon’s post with a 3,800 word essay calling for a slowdown and guardrails on the development of AI. He also told CNN’s Anderson Cooper that he agreed with Coxon more than he disagreed. Amodei wrote in his essay that the risks are serious, even if the benefits could change humanity for the better.
Some in the industry, however, including the CEO of Hugging Face, which was breached by OpenAI’s AI models when they acted without authorization during a test, believe the fears are overblown.
President Donald Trump is set to meet with executives from the industry Tuesday, including Amodei, in a summit aimed at coming to a consensus in the industry. Trump has repeatedly resisted calls to regulate AI and has dismissed concerns as a “hoax.”
AI stocks slide after top industry CEOs call for slowdown of technology’s development
AI giants need to raise a great amount of money to fund their costly development plans, and the massive amount of AI spending among big tech companies on computing infrastructure and talent has sent jitters through Wall Street.
The leaked Anthropic IPO filing sheds light on its financials, revealing that the company lost $42 billion in 2025, according to Reuters. The company plans to spend $518 billion on cloud computing and infrastructure obligations in coming year, and said that nearly a quarter of its revenue last year came from two customers.
Anthropic was last valued at $965 billion in May.
